title: The Phone Doctor
teaser: Everyone on the street brings their broken phones to Malak.
paragraphs: Malak is twenty-two and lives in Sohag. When she was twelve, she dropped her father’s old phone and broke the screen. Instead of crying, she watched a video and fixed it with a tiny screwdriver. Since then, she has been in love with phones.

Now everyone on her street calls her the Phone Doctor. Neighbours bring her phones with broken screens, dead batteries and charging problems. She has a small table in the corner of the living room with tools, a lamp and boxes of tiny screws.

One day, an old woman brings a very old phone. “It doesn’t work,” she says sadly. “But it has the only photos of my son’s wedding.” Malak looks at it. The phone is badly damaged. She is not sure she can save it.

She works on it for three evenings. She cleans the board, replaces the battery and carefully connects new parts. On the third night, the screen lights up. Malak copies all the photos to a memory card.

When the old woman sees the photos on her new phone, she cries and hugs Malak. She wants to pay a lot of money, but Malak takes only the price of the battery. That night, Malak decides to take an evening course in electronic engineering.

a tool for turning screws
broken or hurt
to join two things together

recap: Malak, a teenage phone fixer, saves an old woman’s wedding photos from a broken phone and decides to study electronic engineering.

title: How a Tiny Phone Camera Takes Great Photos
teaser: The lens is smaller than a lentil. The secret is software.
paragraphs: A professional camera has a large lens and a big sensor that collects a lot of light. A phone camera has to fit into a body less than a centimetre thick. Physically, it cannot compete. So how do modern phones take such impressive photos? The answer is mostly software, often called computational photography.

When you press the button, your phone does not take just one picture. It usually captures several frames in a fraction of a second, some darker and some brighter. Then it combines them, keeping the details in the bright sky from one frame and the details in the dark shadows from another. This technique is called HDR, or high dynamic range.

Night mode works in a similar way. The phone takes many frames over a few seconds, aligns them to correct small movements of your hand, and averages them to reduce noise, the grainy dots that appear in dark photos.

Portrait mode uses two cameras or depth sensors, plus artificial intelligence, to estimate which parts of the image are close and which are far. It then blurs the background artificially to imitate the effect of a large professional lens.

Phones also process colours, sharpen edges and smooth skin automatically. This is why two phones can take very different pictures of the same scene. Some photographers prefer to turn these features off and shoot in a raw format, which keeps the original data so they can edit it themselves.

targets.en: a part that notices light, heat or movement
very good; making people admire it
to take a picture or recording of something
to join things together
to guess a number or size carefully
to make something less clear

questions.q: What is computational photography?
How does HDR work?
options: It combines darker and brighter frames

questions.q: How does portrait mode blur the background?
options: It estimates distance and blurs far parts

questions.q: Why do some photographers use raw format?
options: To keep the original data and edit themselves

recap: Phone cameras compensate for tiny lenses with software: HDR combines frames, night mode averages many shots, portrait mode blurs using depth estimates.

title: The App for Grandpa
teaser: Tamer’s grandfather kept forgetting his medicine. Tamer could code.
paragraphs: Tamer is twenty and studies computer science in Ismailia. His grandfather lives with his family. Grandpa has to take three different medicines every day, at different times. He often forgets, and Tamer’s mother worries all the time.
Tamer has an idea. He is learning to build mobile apps. Why not build a simple app for Grandpa? It will show a big picture of the medicine and play a loud sound at the right time.

He works on it every evening for two weeks. There are many errors. The sound does not play. The app closes suddenly. Tamer searches for solutions online and asks questions in a programmers’ group. Slowly, he fixes each problem.

Then he tests it with Grandpa. Grandpa cannot read the small buttons, so Tamer makes them much bigger. Grandpa does not understand the word “Snooze”, so Tamer changes it to “Remind me in 10 minutes” in Arabic.

Now Grandpa never forgets his medicine. He proudly shows the app to his friends at the coffee shop. Two of them ask Tamer for the same app. Tamer smiles. Maybe his first real customers are seventy years old.

targets.en: something you take when you are ill
a mistake
a way to fix a problem
a small part you press on a screen or machine
to help someone remember

title: What Is an API? The Waiter Explanation
teaser: Every app you use talks to other apps. Here is how.
paragraphs: When you open a weather app, it shows you today’s temperature in Alexandria. But the app itself does not have thermometers all over Egypt. It asks another computer, a weather service, for the information. The way these two programs talk to each other is called an API, which stands for Application Programming Interface.

A common way to explain it is a restaurant. You are the customer, and the kitchen is the system that has the food. You cannot walk into the kitchen and cook yourself. Instead, a waiter takes your order, brings it to the kitchen and returns with your food. The API is the waiter: it defines what you can ask for and how the answer will come back.

In practice, a program sends a request to a specific address on the internet, for example asking for the weather in a city. The server checks the request, finds the data and sends back a response, usually in a format called JSON, which is easy for programs to read.

APIs are everywhere. When you pay online, the shop uses a payment company’s API. When an app lets you log in with Google, it uses Google’s API. Even this app uses an API to save your words and send them to your phone.

Most APIs require a key, a long secret code that identifies who is asking. This lets the provider limit how many requests each user can make, charge money, and block abuse. That is why developers must never share their keys publicly.

targets.en: how hot or cold something is
the way two systems or a person and a machine connect
to say exactly what something is
the act of asking for something
an answer
wrong or harmful use

questions.q: What does API stand for?
In the restaurant example, what is the API?
What format do responses often use?
Why should developers never share their keys?
options: The key identifies them and could be abused

recap: An API lets programs request data from each other, like a waiter between customer and kitchen; responses come as JSON and keys must stay secret.

title: Ask Me Anything
teaser: Farida used AI to do her homework. Then her teacher asked one question.
paragraphs: Farida is twenty-five. She works all day and studies for a diploma at night. She has a lot of homework, and she is tired. One night, she discovers an AI chat app. She types her history question, and in five seconds there is a perfect answer.
For two weeks, she uses the app for everything: history, Arabic essays, even English writing. Her marks go up. She feels clever and free.

Then one day, her teacher, Mr. Kamal, reads her essay in front of the class. “This is excellent,” he says. “Farida, can you explain your third point to everyone?” Farida stands up. Her mind is empty. She cannot remember what her essay says.
After class, Mr. Kamal talks to her. He is not angry. “AI is a great tool,” he says. “But if it thinks for you, your brain doesn’t grow. Use it like a teacher, not like a servant.”

So Farida changes the way she uses the app. Now she writes her answer first. Then she asks the AI, “What is wrong with my answer? Explain, but don’t write it for me.” It is slower. But in the final exam, there is no app, and Farida knows the answers herself.

to find something for the first time
a short piece of writing on a topic
to make something clear
a thing you use to do a job

title: How Does an AI Chatbot Write Sentences?
teaser: It does not look up answers in a book. It predicts.
paragraphs: When you chat with an AI assistant, it can feel as if someone is thinking on the other side. In reality, a large language model works in a very different way from a human brain, although the results can be surprisingly human-like.

The model is first trained on an enormous amount of text: books, websites, articles and code. During training, it repeatedly tries to predict the next word, or part of a word, in a sentence. Each time it guesses wrong, its internal settings, called parameters, are adjusted slightly. After billions of these adjustments, it becomes extremely good at predicting what comes next.

Predicting the next word well requires learning a lot about language and the world: grammar, facts, styles, and patterns of reasoning. That is why a model trained only to predict text can also translate, summarise and answer questions.
After this first stage, developers usually train the model further with human feedback, teaching it to be helpful, to follow instructions and to refuse harmful requests.

However, the model does not check a database of verified facts by default. It produces what seems most likely, which is usually right but sometimes completely wrong, a problem called hallucination. That is why it is wise to check important information, especially names, numbers and quotes, and to use AI as a helper rather than an unquestioned source of truth.

targets.en: someone or something that helps you
very big
to say what will happen
to give the main points briefly
to say no

questions.q: What does the model try to do during training?
questions.ar: النموذج بيحاول يعمل إيه وقت التدريب؟

What is hallucination?
options: When the AI produces something wrong that sounds right

recap: Language models learn by predicting the next word in huge text collections, then human feedback; they can hallucinate, so check important facts.

title: The Rooftop Telescope
teaser: In the city, Omar never saw stars. Then he went to the desert.
paragraphs: Omar is twenty-five and works in an office in Cairo. When he looks at the sky at night, he sees only a few stars. The city lights are too strong. But Omar loves space. He watches videos about planets every day.

For his birthday, his uncle gives him a small telescope. Omar is very excited. He takes it to the roof of his building. He points it at the brightest light in the sky. It is not a star. It is Jupiter, and he can see four tiny dots next to it: four of its moons.
Omar wants to see more. His uncle has an idea. “Let’s go to the desert this weekend,” he says. They drive for three hours to a camp near the White Desert, far from the city lights.

When the sun goes down, Omar cannot believe his eyes. The sky is full of stars, thousands and thousands of them. He can see the Milky Way, a bright cloudy line across the sky. His uncle tells him the names of some stars. Some of these names come from Arabic.

Omar does not sleep much that night. He looks through the telescope until his eyes hurt. In the morning, he says to his uncle, “One day, I want to visit a real observatory.” His uncle laughs. “Then you will need a bigger telescope.”

a big round object that moves around a star

title: Why Is the Sky Blue — and Sunsets Orange?
teaser: Sunlight contains every colour. The air chooses which ones you see.
paragraphs: Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour is light with a different wavelength: red has the longest waves and blue and violet the shortest. You can see this mixture separate when light passes through a prism or raindrops.

When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it hits tiny molecules of gas, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter light in all directions, but they scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. So blue light bounces around the sky and reaches our eyes from every direction. That is why the sky looks blue.

If violet light is scattered even more, why is the sky not violet? Part of the reason is that sunlight contains less violet, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.

At sunset, the sun is low, so its light travels through much more air before it reaches us. Most of the blue light is scattered away along the path, and the longer wavelengths, orange and red, are what remain. Dust and pollution can make sunsets even more colourful.
On the Moon, which has no atmosphere, there is nothing to scatter the light. Astronauts see a black sky even during the day, with the Sun shining like a bright white disc.

targets.en: different things mixed together
the distance between waves of light or sound
the layer of gases around a planet
to send in many different directions
reacting easily to something

questions.q: What is sunlight made of?

options: Air molecules scatter blue light strongly

questions.q: Why are sunsets orange and red?
options: Light travels through more air and blue is scattered away

questions.q: What colour is the sky on the Moon?

recap: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths, so the sky is blue; at sunset light crosses more air leaving orange and red; the Moon’s sky is black.

title: How Does a Bank Card Work?
teaser: You tap your card and pay. What happens in those two seconds?
paragraphs: You are in a supermarket. You tap your bank card on a small machine, wait two seconds, and the machine says “Approved”. It looks simple, but in those two seconds, many computers talk to each other.
First, the machine reads a chip in your card. The chip creates a special code for this payment only. This makes it very difficult for criminals to copy your card.
Then the machine sends the information to the supermarket’s bank. That bank sends it to the card network, like Visa or Mastercard. The network sends it to your bank.

Your bank checks two important things. Is the card real? Do you have enough money? If the answer is yes, your bank sends back “approved”. The message travels back the same way to the machine in the supermarket.

The money does not move immediately. Later, usually at the end of the day, the banks send the money between them. That is why sometimes a payment appears in your app a day later. All of this happens thousands of times every second around the world.

recap: Tapping a card sends a one-time chip code through the shop’s bank and card network to your bank, which approves it; money moves later.

title: Why Do We Have Time Zones?
teaser: Before trains, every town had its own time. That caused chaos.
paragraphs: For most of history, every town set its clocks by the sun. Noon was simply the moment when the sun was highest in the sky. Because the Earth turns, noon in Alexandria came a few minutes earlier than noon in Cairo. Nobody minded, because travelling between them took a long time.

Railways changed everything. In the nineteenth century, trains made it possible to travel hundreds of kilometres in a few hours. Suddenly, local times became a problem. Timetables were confusing, and in some countries, stations showed several different times at once.

The solution was standard time. In 1884, representatives from many countries met in Washington and agreed to use Greenwich, in London, as the starting line, or prime meridian. The world could be divided into twenty-four zones, each roughly one hour apart, because the Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour.

In practice, time zones follow political borders, not perfect lines. China, which is very wide, uses one single time zone. Some countries use half-hour differences, and some change their clocks in summer, a system called daylight saving time, to have more daylight in the evening.

Today, time zones affect everyday life in surprising ways: online meetings with people abroad, football matches broadcast late at night, and the jet lag travellers feel when their body clock is still on home time.

title: The Factory Newsletter
teaser: Rania’s first story was about a broken water fountain. It changed more than she expected.
paragraphs: Rania is twenty-four and works in the office of a big factory in Tanta. She wants to be a journalist one day. The factory does not have a newsletter, so she asks the manager if she can start one. He says yes, but only one page every month.

For her first story, Rania looks for a real problem. She finds one quickly: the water fountain in the workers’ area has been broken for three months. Workers are thirsty, especially in the hot afternoons.

Rania does not only write her opinion. She asks questions like a real journalist. She interviews ten workers, the cleaner and the office secretary. She takes photos. She learns that the factory asked for a repair, but the papers were lost.
Her article is short and clear. The title is “Three Months Without Water”. She prints thirty copies and puts them on the walls. Managers read it on their way to meetings.
One week later, a worker comes and fixes the fountain. The manager calls Rania to his office. She is worried. But he smiles and says, “Good journalism. What is your next story?”

title: How to Spot Fake News in Five Questions
teaser: A shocking post in the family group. Before you share it, ask these.
paragraphs: Every day, millions of messages are shared in family groups and on social media. Some are true, some are partly true, and some are completely invented. False information spreads faster than corrections, often because it is surprising or makes people angry. Before you share something, it helps to ask five simple questions.

First: who is the source? Is the post from a known news organisation, an official account, or a random page with no history? A screenshot of a headline is not a source; try to find the original article.
Second: is anyone else reporting it? If something truly important happened, several independent outlets will usually cover it. If only one unknown page has the story, be careful.

Third: when was it published? Old news is often shared again as if it were new. A photo of a flood from ten years ago can be presented as happening today. A reverse image search can show where and when a photo first appeared.

Fourth: does it try to make you emotional? Headlines with lots of capital letters, words like “shocking” and urgent requests to share immediately are warning signs. Fifth: does it sound too perfect? If a story confirms exactly what you already believed, check it twice. Taking thirty seconds to verify a message is a small but powerful way to protect your family and friends.
